text.description:
The Eiffel Tower is the lattice iron tower on the Champ de Mars that most people picture when they think of Paris. Gustave Eiffel's company built it between 1887 and 1889 as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair. Parisians nicknamed it "La dame de fer", the Iron Lady. It stands 330 metres tall, with a square base 125 metres on each side, and it is still the tallest structure in Paris.

The phone icon on the map is about 600 m north-west of the subject. That distance helps a phone photographer. You are far enough back to fit the whole tower in one frame, from the four legs and arches at the base to the aerial at the top. You are still close enough for the ironwork to look sharp and detailed. The tower's shape is simple and symmetrical, so a straight, steady shot usually looks good.

Hold the phone level and use the gridlines to keep the tower upright. Leave a little space above the tip, because tilting up to fit the top in makes the legs lean inwards. If people are walking in front of you, wait for a gap or include them to give a sense of scale. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, since the tower looks quite different with sky around it than when cropped tightly on the girders.

Tickets are sold for going up the tower.

text.description:
The Arc de Triomphe stands at the western end of the Champs-Élysées, in the middle of the big star-shaped junction now called Place Charles de Gaulle, where twelve avenues meet. Napoleon commissioned it in 1806 after the victory at Austerlitz, but it was not finished until 1836. It is about 49.5 m tall and nearly 45 m wide, so it is a big, simple shape that is easy to recognise in a photo. Beneath the vault lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier from the First World War, marked by an eternal flame. The arch is also the central point of the Axe historique, the long line of monuments and grand streets running from the Louvre out to La Défense.

It photographs well because the Champs-Élysées leads the eye straight to it. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. That is far enough to fit the whole monument in the frame, with the tree-lined pavements and traffic leading towards it. The sculpture and engraved names are easier to see up close, so walk nearer afterwards for detail shots. Keep an eye on traffic and other visitors on the pavements, and keep your phone held firmly near busy kerbs. If you plan to go inside the arch, check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Louvre Pyramid is the glass entrance to the Louvre Museum, set in the palace's main courtyard, the Cour Napoléon. Architect I. M. Pei designed it, and it was completed in 1989 as part of the Grand Louvre project. Three smaller pyramids stand around it, and on three sides there are low triangular reflecting pools with fountains. That mix of clear glass and old palace stonework is why it photographs so well: the pyramid reflects the sky and the palace wings, and the pools add a second layer of reflections.

It is 21.6 metres tall, with a square base 34 metres along each side. It is made of 673 glass panes (603 rhombus-shaped, 70 triangular), and the Louvre itself confirms that count. The pale, repeating diamond pattern gives you strong lines to work with, and the older buildings behind it make a good backdrop.

The phone icon on the map is about 200 m west of the subject. From there you see it at a distance, with the palace around it, rather than filling the frame. That works best with your phone's zoom. For close-up shots of the glass pattern, walk into the courtyard and shoot upwards. Bear in mind that this is the museum's main entrance, so it may be busy around the base. Check the official Louvre site before you go if you plan to go inside.

Keep the phone level so the pyramid's base stays straight. For a close-up, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and tilt up slightly. Keep the base level so the glass diamonds make clean diagonal lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pyramid to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright glass and sky keep their detail. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving past the pools.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light and fewer people. After dark, try night mode with the phone held steady against a wall or railing, if the pyramid is lit when you visit.

text.description:
The Catacombs of Paris are a vast underground ossuary holding the remains of more than six million people. They were made inside old limestone quarries beneath the Left Bank. From the late 1780s, remains were carried here by night from the city's overcrowded cemeteries, in covered wagons. The ossuary was opened to visitors in 1874, and since 2013 it has been one of the City of Paris museums run by Paris Musées.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the story behind the place as much as the view. Above ground, the entrance sits right beside Place Denfert-Rochereau, the area where the visitor accesses were built. A photo of the entrance area, with a little of the square around it, is an easy way to record the visit, and you can take it before or after your time below. The old city gate known as the Barrière d'Enfer, the "Gate of Hell", stood here. It makes a good detail to mention in a caption.

Bring a simple plan. Take a few frames of the entrance from different distances, then a close detail or two. Photography rules underground can differ from the street, so check the official site before you go and respect any signs once inside. Wipe your lens before you start, as phone lenses pick up smudges easily, and keep your phone steady against a wall or railing when light is low.

text.description: Notre-Dame is the medieval cathedral on the Île de la Cité, an island in the Seine, and it is one of the most recognisable buildings in Paris. Work began in 1163 and was largely finished by 1260. It is considered one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture, and its flying buttresses, big rose windows and richly carved figures all reward a closer look with your phone. The cathedral was badly damaged by fire in April 2019, when much of the roof and the spire were lost. It reopened in December 2024 after about three years of reconstruction, so you are photographing a freshly restored building. In the early 21st century it drew about 12 million visitors a year, which makes it the most visited monument in Paris. Expect people in your frame. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m north-west of the subject. That is far enough back to fit the twin towers and the front in one shot, with room for the sky above. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the front, and turn it sideways if you want the square or the crowds in the picture. Move closer and zoom for the carved doorways and the rose window. Wipe your lens first, as pocket fluff softens a big stone façade more than you would expect.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid to late afternoon or early evening is a good bet, when the west-facing front catches warmer light. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in the shot.

text.description: Sacré-Cœur is the white-domed basilica that crowns the hill of Montmartre, and it is one of the easiest big buildings in Paris to photograph with a phone. The pale stone stands out against the sky, and the rounded domes give you a strong, simple shape even from a distance. It sits at the very top of the hill, so it is visible from many parts of the city. The basilica was designed by Paul Abadie, whose plan was chosen from seventy-seven proposals. Building started in 1875 and the church was finished in 1914, then formally consecrated in 1919. The hilltop ground was unstable, so eighty-three deep wells had to be dug and filled with rock and concrete to carry the weight. Five more architects followed Abadie, which is why the finished building mixes several hands. Today it is one of the most visited places in the capital. Start wide to take in the whole front and the domes, then move in for the carved doorways and the dome. Check for people walking through the foreground before you shoot, and wait a moment if you want a cleaner view. Because it is an active church, be discreet with your phone near the entrances.

text.description: The Palais Garnier is the grand Paris opera house on the Place de l'Opéra, in the 9th arrondissement. It was built between 1861 and 1875 for Napoleon III and seats 1,979 people. Today the Paris Opera company uses it mainly for ballet. It has been a protected monument historique since 1923, and it is also known as the setting of The Phantom of the Opera. It photographs well because the main façade is a busy mix of coloured marble, columns, sculpture and gilded figures. Seventeen different materials were used on it. The two gilded groups, L'Harmonie and La Poésie, stand at the top of the left and right ends of the façade and catch the light. Lower down, between the columns, are gilded busts of composers such as Mozart and Beethoven. The façade reaches 32 metres, and the stage tower behind it rises to 56 metres. Because the building is so wide and so detailed, plan two kinds of picture: one of the whole front, and a few close-ups of the sculpture. The Dance by Carpeaux, on the base of the façade, makes a good close-up. The building closes the view along the Avenue de l'Opéra, so a straight-on, symmetrical shot works well. Traffic and people move around the square all day, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest one. For any look inside, check the official site before you go.

text.description: The Sainte-Chapelle is a royal chapel on the Île de la Cité, built between 1238 and 1248 for King Louis IX. He had it made to hold his collection of relics of the Passion, including the Crown of Thorns. It stands in the courtyard of the old Palais de la Cité, once the main home of the Kings of France, and it is one of the few buildings left from that royal palace. The chapel has two levels. The lower one was for courtiers, servants and soldiers, and the upper one was kept for the royal family and their guests. It measures about 36 m long, 17 m wide and 42.5 m high, which is large for a chapel. The upper windows hold one of the biggest collections of original 13th-century stained glass anywhere, and the west front has a Flamboyant rose window added around the end of the 15th century. On a phone it gives you two very different pictures. Outside, you can photograph the tall stone Gothic outline. Inside, you can capture the walls of coloured glass. Stand back as far as the courtyard allows, keep the phone level, and use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. Inside, focus on the glass rather than the dim stonework.

Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the windows. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single panels of glass or details of the carving.

The Moulin Rouge is a cabaret on the Boulevard de Clichy, topped with a red windmill that is easy to spot from the street. It is best known as the birthplace of the modern can-can, and Toulouse-Lautrec's posters helped make its name famous.

text.description:
The Jardin du Luxembourg is a large, calm garden in the 6th arrondissement, built around a wide octagonal pond, the Grand Bassin. Marie de' Medici began it in 1612 when she built the Luxembourg Palace as her new home, and the garden is now owned by the French Senate, which meets in the palace. It covers 23 hectares, so there is plenty of room to wander and choose your angle.

It photographs well because everything is laid out in clear, formal lines: gravel paths, lawns, flowerbeds, tree-lined walks and raised terraces with balustrades. Statues of French queens and other figures stand along those terraces and make good foregrounds. Children sail model boats on the basin, which adds colour and a bit of life to a wide shot. The Medici Fountain, dating from 1620, is a quieter, shadier subject at the eastern side of the garden.

For phone photos, use the long views along the paths and the basin edge. Keep the horizon level, because the straight lines show any tilt. Move in close for details such as a statue against the trees, or a small boat on the water. Take a few steps sideways to keep other visitors from blocking the view, and be patient on busy days. Avoid zooming in too far, as that softens the detail on a phone.

text.description:
Place de la Concorde is the largest square in Paris, covering 7.6 hectares, and it is hard to cross without wanting to take a photo. It sits at the eastern end of the Champs-Élysées, with the Tuileries Garden on one side and the Seine on the other. At its centre stands the Luxor Obelisk, a gift from Egypt that was raised here in October 1836 in front of a big crowd. Around the square are two grand fountains, rings of lamp-topped columns and eight statues, each representing a French city. Two matching palatial buildings with identical façades, designed by Ange-Jacques Gabriel, close off the north side. The square began as a setting for a statue of Louis XV, was a major stage for the French Revolution, and was renamed Concorde in 1795 as a gesture of reconciliation.

It photographs well because of the scale. You get a tall central obelisk, fountains, lamps and long open lines in one view, with grand buildings behind. Because the square is so wide, a single photo can only say part of it, so take a few. Start with one wide shot to show the whole setting. Then take a closer one of the obelisk against the sky, and another of a fountain or a statue. Keep the phone level so the tall obelisk and the buildings do not lean. Take care near the roads around the square and cross only at the marked crossings.

text.description:
The Palais de Chaillot is the broad, curved building that stands on Chaillot Hill, in the Trocadéro area. It was built for the 1937 International Exhibition. The architects partly rebuilt an older palace from 1878, keeping its two curving wings and adding taller sections in front. The old central hall and towers were taken down, leaving a wide open esplanade in their place. That gap gives a clear line of sight from Place du Trocadéro towards the Eiffel Tower and beyond.

It photographs well because of its scale and its calm, symmetrical shape. The pale stone wings sweep round in a wide arc, and there are sculpture groups along the top edge. Gilded figures stand on the terrace, and the buildings are decorated with quotations by Paul Valéry. In 1948 the United Nations General Assembly met here and adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. A stone on the esplanade marks the event, and the space is called the esplanade of human rights.

On a phone, start with the wide view, then move in on details such as the sculptures and gilded figures. The palace is big, so give yourself room and keep the phone level so the long horizontal lines look straight. Today the wings hold several museums and a theatre, so there may be people coming and going near the entrances. Be patient and wait for a gap if you want a cleaner frame.

name: Les Invalides
label: Les Invalides
camera_source: Commons cluster (68 photos).

text.description: Les Invalides is a grand complex of buildings in the 7th arrondissement. Louis XIV ordered it in 1670 as a home and hospital for veterans of his wars. It now holds the army museum and the tomb of Napoleon, and it still includes a retirement home for former soldiers. For a phone photographer, the appeal is scale and symmetry. The long façade facing the Seine is 196 metres wide, and the Dôme rises above it to 107 metres, making it the tallest church building in Paris and taller than Notre Dame. In front lies the wide, open Esplanade des Invalides, which gives you the clear distance you need to fit the whole building into one frame. The esplanade is open ground, so there is plenty of space to move around, and the buildings stood in as a backdrop for several sports at the 2024 Olympics. The Dôme sits in the centre of your view with the long front spreading out on either side, which makes a naturally balanced picture. Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines of the façade stay straight. A strip of lawn or path in the foreground adds depth and stops the shot looking flat. If you want to go inside, for the museum or the tomb, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Les Invalides is in the 7th arrondissement, south of the Seine.
text.directions_text: Varenne (Métro line 13) is the nearest station, about 179 metres from the Invalides, which lies to the west of it. That is about 3 minutes on foot. La Tour Maubourg (Métro line 8) is about 242 metres away, with the Invalides to the south-east, which is about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the façade and the open esplanade in front. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view centred on the Dôme. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the dome and the lantern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Stay on the central axis of the complex for a symmetrical picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the Dôme up with the central vertical line. Keep the phone level so the horizontal lines of the façade do not lean. Include some path or lawn in the foreground for depth. For a more intimate shot, use telephoto and fill the frame with the dome alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Panorama mode can work for the full width, but hold the phone steady and upright as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the esplanade is usually less crowded. Use the exposure slider on a bright day.

text.access_note: The Esplanade des Invalides is a wide public open space; the museum, the Dôme and Napoleon's tomb may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Centre Pompidou
label: Centre Pompidou
camera_source: Commons cluster (17 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/55503397: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Centre Pompidou' (211 m across).

text.description:
The Centre Pompidou is the building that turns a gallery inside out. The structure, the pipes and the circulation elements are all on the outside, so the facade looks like a giant, colourful machine. It was designed by Richard Rogers, Su Rogers, Renzo Piano and Gianfranco Franchini, and opened on 31 January 1977. The design was chosen from 681 competition entries. The colours were part of the plan from the start: green for plumbing, blue for climate control, yellow for electrics and red for circulation and safety equipment. That makes it an easy subject for a phone, because the bold colours and strong lines stand out even in flat light.

The centre houses a large public library and the Musée National d'Art Moderne, the largest museum of modern art in Europe. It sits in the Beaubourg area, with an open plaza in front. Please note that it closed for a major renovation in 2025 and is expected to reopen in 2030. Scaffolding, hoardings or fenced-off areas may affect your view, so check the official site before you go. Use the wide view to include the whole structure, then switch to a tighter zoom for details such as the tubes and the criss-crossing steel. Straight lines look best when the phone is held level.
text.geographic_location: The Centre Pompidou is in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement. The Place Georges Pompidou, an open plaza, lies in front of it.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Rambuteau (Métro line 11), about 3 minutes on foot, with the building to the south-west of the station. You can also use Hôtel de Ville (Métro line 1 and Métro line 11), about 5 minutes on foot, with the building to the north. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are close and the building is large. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and a 2x-5x telephoto, if your phone has one, for details of the pipes and tubes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. If the plaza is partly closed, stay at the nearest open spot and check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the horizontal floors up with them to keep the facade straight. Fill the frame with the pattern of tubes and steel, and keep a few people or a lamp-post in the foreground for scale. Then zoom in on one colourful section for a graphic close-up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If the screen glare is strong, take two or three frames and pick the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight shows the colours cleanly, and late afternoon can add warmth to the steel. Early in the day is likely to be quieter. After dark, night mode can work if the building is lit, but hold your phone steady.

text.access_note: The Centre Pompidou is closed for renovation, with reopening expected in 2030, so check the official site before you go for what you can see and reach.

name: Panthéon
label: Panthéon
camera_source: Commons cluster (106 photos). Moved 55 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 50 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/16407465: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pantheon' (147 m across).
notes: Only 'pantheon paris' counted: 'pantheon' alone (361,800) mostly means Rome's Pantheon.

text.description: The Panthéon crowns the hill of Montagne Sainte-Geneviève in the Latin Quarter, and its tall stone dome and columned front make it one of the easiest buildings in Paris to photograph. It began as a church. Louis XV wanted a grander home for the relics of Saint Genevieve, Paris's patron saint, and the architect Jacques-Germain Soufflot designed it. Building ran from 1758 to 1790, and neither man lived to see it finished. By then the Revolution had begun, and the building became a mausoleum for France's distinguished citizens. It is an early example of Neoclassical architecture, and it stands about 83 metres high and 110 metres long. That is why it looks so commanding from the open square in front. What you see from outside is the outermost of three domes set inside one another, built of stone and covered in lead. Expect to tilt the phone upwards, and expect the dome and the full width of the building not to fit in one shot unless you use the widest lens. Look for the columns of the portico, the pale stone against the sky, and the long sweep of the square. People wandering through the square also add a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The Panthéon is in the 5th arrondissement, in the Latin Quarter, on the Place du Panthéon on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève.
text.directions_text: From Cardinal Lemoine (Métro line 10), the Panthéon is about 7 minutes on foot, to the west. Maubert - Mutualité (Métro line 10) is also close, about 8 minutes on foot, with the Panthéon to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the building and the dome together from this close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the columns and portico. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the details high up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. If the dome gets cut off, take a few steps back and use the ultra-wide (0.5x).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and use them to keep the columns upright. Tilting the phone up makes the vertical lines lean inwards, so stand back and keep the phone as level as you can, then leave a little sky above the dome. Try one shot with people in the foreground to show the size of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the pale stone. Take a couple of frames at different exposures and keep the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone. Midday sun can flatten the façade, so use the exposure slider then.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the building can be photographed freely, but visiting the interior is likely to be ticketed and may have restrictions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shakespeare and Company
label: Shakespeare & Co
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/251373380: the OpenStreetMap point 'Shakespeare and Company'.

text.description:
Shakespeare and Company is a long-standing English-language bookshop on the Left Bank. George Whitman, an American, opened it in 1951 under the name Le Mistral. In 1964 he renamed it in honour of Sylvia Beach's earlier shop of the same name, which had closed in 1941. The building stands on the site of a 16th-century monastery. The shop is also known for its beds tucked between the shelves, where aspiring writers have stayed in exchange for helping out. An estimated 30,000 people have slept there since 1951.

It photographs well because it has real character. The shopfront, the book displays outside and the lettering above the door make a good picture of a working bookshop. Notre-Dame and the Seine are only steps away, so the street has a strong Paris feel. Next door is a small park, Square René-Viviani, and a café that opened in 2015.

For a phone shot, stand at the phone icon on the map. From there the shop is about 19 metres away to the south, so you can see the whole frontage with the street around it. Keep people in the frame if you like, as they give a sense of scale. Wait for a gap if you want the front clear. The shop is a busy place, so be polite to staff and customers.
text.geographic_location: In the 5th arrondissement on the Left Bank, at 37 rue de la Bûcherie, close to Place Saint-Michel. It is a few steps from the Seine and Notre-Dame, beside Square René-Viviani.
text.directions_text: From Saint-Michel Notre-Dame (RER B and RER C), the shop is about 134 m to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. From Cluny-La Sorbonne (Métro line 10), the shop is about 268 m to the north-east, about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the shopfront. If the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front in. Keep the phone level, because ultra-wide stretches lines near the edges. A 2x telephoto shot works well for details such as the lettering, the book stalls and the signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the shopfront with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Include a little of the street in the foreground to show where it is. For a closer shot, zoom to 2x and frame the sign and the book displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the shopfront to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the details do not wash out. Take a few shots while people pass, then choose the one with the clearest view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, when fewer people are around, is usually easiest for a clear view of the frontage. Evening light can also look good when the shop windows are lit.

text.access_note: The shop is a working bookshop and the street outside is public, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules on photography inside.
